How Colorado property tax is calculated

Three numbers make the bill. First the assessor estimates what the property is actually worth. Then a rate that depends on the property's class converts that into assessed value. Finally every taxing body that covers the parcel applies its own levy, and the levies are added together. One mill equals a tenth of a cent, which is why 13.980 mills appears as 0.013980.

Use on January 1 decides the class. Houses are valued by the market approach alone, which means recent comparable sales. Commercial and personal property can also be valued by what it costs to replace or what income it produces.

Who does what: assessor, taxing districts, treasurer

Different offices handle valuation, rates and collection, so a seller may need to call more than one number.

  • Assessor: locates, classifies and values every parcel, mails the valuation notices and rules on protests.
  • Taxing authorities: county commissioners, city councils, school boards and special district boards each decide the revenue they need and set a levy to raise it.
  • Board of equalization: the county body that hears appeals of assessor decisions.
  • Higher appeals: arbitrators, district court or the Board of Assessment Appeals take cases from the county board.
  • Treasurer: mails the statement and takes payment. El Paso County sends statements to the owner of record on the tax roll, and a statement that never arrives is no excuse for paying late.

With 64 counties there are 64 assessors and 64 treasurers, and Denver and Broomfield run city and county government together. Call the offices for the county where the house sits.

2026 assessment rates by property type

Each class of property has its own assessment rate, and houses get the lowest. In 2026 a residential parcel is assessed at 6.8% for local government levies and 7.05% for school districts.

Classification (2026)Assessment rate
Residential, local government6.8%
Residential, schools7.05%
Vacant land26%
Commercial improved25%
Commercial other26%
Industrial26%
Agricultural25%
State assessed26%

Owners of vacant lots, or of rentals the assessor treats as commercial, should check the class printed on the notice of valuation. A wrong class means a wrong rate and a bigger bill.

When Colorado reassesses

Real property gets a new valuation in odd-numbered years only, while personal property is revalued yearly. Notices of valuation for real property go out by May 1.

Values for tax years 2025 and 2026 come from sales between January 1, 2023 and June 30, 2024, and the state permits earlier six-month windows where sales are scarce. El Paso County applies its 2025 values to tax year 2026 using a 2023 base year, and in even-numbered years it mails notices only to parcels that changed.

Because of that lag, the price in your contract does not set the buyer's bill. The assessor's value does, and a price far above or below it changes nothing until the next reappraisal.

Due dates and penalties

Statements are mailed soon after January 1. Owners choose between one payment by April 30 and two halves, due the last day of February and June 15. The split is not available on a bill of $25 or less, which is due in full by April 30.

Treasurers enforce these dates county by county. In El Paso County late payments accrue 1% interest per month, with no grace period and no partial payments, and anything still unpaid after June 15 is delinquent. From September 30 on, the office takes only cash or certified funds, with no personal checks and no postmark credit.

Colorado collects unpaid real estate tax by selling a tax lien, not the deed. El Paso County holds that sale every fall, online through RealAuction. The treasurer can tell you how long the redemption period lasts afterward.

How to appeal your assessment

The path begins at the assessor's office, moves to the county board of equalization, and can end at the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or binding arbitration. El Paso County posts its calendar, so it works as a model.

  • At the assessor: file between May 1 and June 8 and expect a Notice of Determination by August 15.
  • At the board of equalization: hearings take place over Teams in July and August, and the real property protest date is in mid July.
  • At the hearing: you and the assessor get 10 minutes each, and you must prove the value you claim.
  • After the hearing: a written decision comes within five business days.
  • Further appeal: file within 30 days of the postmark on the board's decision.

Evidence must be market data from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024 for the 2025 and 2026 values. Repair estimates, an independent appraisal and photos of conditions that pull value down all count. Other counties run on different forms and dates, so read your own assessor's notice.

Exemptions and deferrals

Three programs matter most: the senior exemption, the disabled veteran exemption and the senior deferral. The senior exemption takes half of the first $200,000 of a primary residence's actual value off the tax base, if the state funds it. Applicants must be 65 or older and have owned and lived in the home for 10 years in a row, and the assessor wants the form by July 15.

  • Veteran with a disability and Gold Star spouse: the same 50% of the first $200,000, with a July 1 filing date.
  • Qualified senior primary residence classification: covers tax years 2025 and 2026 for former exemption holders who moved, with a March 15 filing date.
  • Senior deferral: open to anyone 65 or older who applies with the county treasurer from January 1 to April 1, and it has to be renewed yearly.

The state treasurer effectively lends the deferred amount and records a lien. The loan comes due on a sale or transfer of title, and also on death, on a move for reasons other than health, or when the home is rented. A seller with a deferral should order a payoff figure before closing.

Why equal homes get different bills

Levies differ by district, and every house belongs to its own mix. The El Paso County list for tax year 2025, billed in 2026, runs from 2.938 mills for Pikes Peak Library District and 3.009 for the City of Colorado Springs, through 6.857 for the county, up to school districts at 37.695 (Colorado Springs District 11), 45.459 (Academy District 20) and 57.682 (Widefield District 3).

Two houses a few miles apart can land in different school and fire districts and pay different totals, and metro districts in newer subdivisions add still more. Your own tax statement lists the entities that apply.

Taxes at closing

Before signing, have the title company report where this year's taxes stand. The treasurer bills whoever is the owner of record, and some mortgage servicers collect taxes in escrow while others do not, so ask your lender which applies.

Hail and wildfire damage can lower what a buyer will pay. An owner behind on tax with a damaged roof can ask for an as is cash offer instead of paying for repairs first, and closing then pays the back tax out of the proceeds.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the Colorado property tax due date?

Pay by April 30 in one payment, or split it into halves due the last day of February and June 15. A bill of $25 or less must be paid whole by April 30.

How often does Colorado reassess property?

Real property is revalued in odd-numbered years and notices go out by May 1, while personal property is revalued every year.

What interest applies to late Colorado property tax?

The county decides. El Paso County charges 1% per month from the first day late, and taxes unpaid after June 15 are delinquent.

Can I get a property tax break as a Colorado senior?

Possibly. Owners 65 or older who have lived in and owned the home 10 years running can have half of the first $200,000 of actual value exempted, if the state funds it. Apply to the county assessor by July 15.

What happens to a senior tax deferral when I sell?

The deferral comes due on a sale or title transfer. Because the deferred tax and interest sit as a lien, closing pays them out of your proceeds.

What the Colorado homestead exemption protects

The exemption shields part of the equity in your home from creditors who hold a court judgment. It is a different thing from the property tax breaks for seniors, though people confuse the two all the time.

Under C.R.S. 38-41-201, a homestead is exempt from execution and attachment for debts, contracts and civil obligations, up to a set amount of actual cash value above any liens in place when a levy happens. The protected amounts are:

Who occupies the homeProtected amount
An owner or the owner's family$250,000
An owner, spouse or dependent who is elderly or disabled$350,000

Elderly means age sixty or older. Disabled means a physical or mental impairment that substantially keeps the person from useful work in any job that exists in the community and fits their competence. Dollar limits can change, so confirm the figures with the current statute or an attorney before you rely on them.

Do I have to file anything to claim it?

Usually no. Section 38-41-202 says the exemption is created automatically and can be claimed once the home is occupied and is the right kind of homestead.

One older rule still sits in the statute. The exemption cannot be claimed against an obligation incurred before July 1, 1975, unless the owner recorded a written homestead statement with the county clerk and recorder. That date makes it a niche issue today.

A recorded statement does change one thing. When an owner or spouse records the instrument, both spouses must sign to convey or encumber the property. With no recording, a homestead that arises automatically can be conveyed or encumbered by the owner alone, with no other signature needed.

If you are selling, a short checklist helps:

  • Search the county records for a recorded homestead declaration.
  • If one exists, plan for both spouses to sign the deed.
  • If none exists, only the owner of record needs to sign.

The home must be lived in

Section 38-41-203 makes the property exempt only while the owner or the owner's family occupies it as a home.

That matters for a house you are about to sell. A house left empty after a move, or one rented out, may no longer qualify. If a judgment creditor is in the picture, the date you moved out can matter, and a lawyer should read the facts before anyone counts on the protection. For tenant-occupied properties, the eviction and landlord rules are the better place to start.

When a creditor tries to force a sale

A creditor has hurdles to clear first. Under C.R.S. 38-41-206, the creditor must file an affidavit with the county clerk and recorder and with the sheriff or other officer who would levy. The affidavit must include:

  • A description of the homestead and the name of the claimant.
  • The fair market value of the property.
  • A statement that value minus prior liens is above the exemption amount the claimant qualifies for.
  • A statement that no earlier execution from the same judgment has been levied.
  • A second affidavit from a professionally qualified independent appraiser with the same value information.

If the winning bid at the sale does not exceed seventy percent of the appraiser's fair market value, the proceedings end. The officer records a release of all levies, the person who started the case pays the costs, and the owner's title is not harmed.

If a sale does go through, the money is paid out in this order:

  1. Prior liens and encumbrances.
  2. The homestead claimant, up to the exemption amount.
  3. Costs and expenses of the sale.
  4. The judgment.
  5. Anything left over, back to the claimant.

A judgment creditor who is the winning bidder must pay cash for the exemption plus costs, and cannot apply the exempt amount against the judgment.

Protection for sale proceeds

The money from a voluntary sale is protected for a limited time. C.R.S. 38-41-207 exempts the proceeds from execution or attachment for three years after you receive them, as long as you keep the money separate so it can always be identified.

The same protection reaches the exempt amount when the owner sells, proceeds of a sale under section 38-41-206, and insurance money for destroyed homestead property held to restore or replace it.

There is also a carryover. If you use the proceeds to buy another home, the exemption you had on the old house applies to the new one. It does not work against a vendor's lien or the holder of a purchase money mortgage on the new property.

If a creditor is pressing while you sell, do not drop the closing check into a general account. A separate account keeps the money traceable, which is what the statute asks for.

Homestead exemption versus the senior property tax exemption

The homestead exemption is a creditor shield. The senior property tax exemption lowers a tax bill. They sit in different parts of the law and different offices run them.

County assessors take applications for the senior exemption on a yearly cycle, and the application window opens January 1. Ask your county assessor for the current year's form, and if you plan to sell during the year, ask how a sale affects an application that is already filed.

Property taxes when a Colorado house is sold

Colorado lets the taxpayer pay the property tax bill in full or in two installments, and section 39-10-104.5 sets the schedule. Any split between buyer and seller is a term of the sale contract.

Paying in full is due on or before April 30, with no interest through that date. Paying in halves means the first half is due the last day of February and the second half on June 15. Interest runs at one percent per month once a payment is late. No installments are allowed on a total under $25, which must be paid in full by April 30.

Confirm the balance and any delinquent interest with the county treasurer before you set a closing date, so nothing unexpected comes out of the proceeds.

Recording fee on the deed

Besides ordinary recording fees, a deed filed with the county clerk and recorder carries a documentary fee. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102 it is one cent for each $100 of consideration, and no fee applies when the consideration is $500 or less. Whoever offers the deed for recording pays it.

If you are selling a house that has a judgment or lien attached, we are glad to walk through the numbers with you, and we suggest a Colorado attorney for the legal questions.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Colorado homestead exemption protect?

$250,000 for a home occupied by an owner or the owner's family, and $350,000 when the occupant is an elderly or disabled owner, spouse or dependent. Elderly means sixty or older.

Do I need to record a homestead declaration?

No. The exemption arises automatically if the occupancy and property type rules are met. Recording a statement matters only for older debts, and it changes who must sign a deed.

Does the homestead exemption stop me from selling my house?

No. It limits what a judgment creditor can collect from the home but does not block a voluntary sale. A recorded declaration means both spouses must sign the deed.

How long are the sale proceeds protected?

Three years after you receive them, if you keep them separate and identifiable. If you buy another home with the money, the same exemption carries over to it.

Can a creditor force the sale of my home for any price?

No. If the winning bid is seventy percent or less of the appraiser's fair market value, the proceedings end and the creditor pays the costs.

Colorado estate and inheritance tax

Colorado levies neither. Its estate tax was effectively wiped out for anyone who died after December 31, 2004, and today nobody has to file a Colorado estate tax return. No estate tax revenue has come in since fiscal year 2013-14. For a family with an inherited house to sell, the real questions are federal estate tax and income tax on any profit.

The one carve-out is Form DR 1210, which matters only for a death that happened before December 31, 2004.

An heir who lives elsewhere should ask the estate attorney about the home state, because some states tax what a beneficiary receives and the heir's own state rules would apply, not Colorado's.

Why Colorado dropped the tax

Colorado's tax was a piggyback on a federal credit. Lose the credit and the tax disappears. The state enacted an inheritance tax in 1927. Lawmakers replaced it in 1980 with an estate tax that matched the federal "state death tax credit" on returns filed until 2005.

Federal law cut that credit between 2002 and 2004 and then ended it. Colorado sets no exemptions of its own, because the tax was never more than a share of the federal credit. If Congress ever brought the credit back, a Colorado estate tax could start collecting again, but nothing like that is in place today.

Ending the credit did not shrink the total estate tax paid nationally. It moved the revenue from Colorado to the federal government.

Federal estate tax for Colorado heirs

Federal estate tax reaches only very large estates. Whether a return is due turns on the year of death, and the filing line is the total of the gross estate, adjusted taxable gifts and the specific gift tax exemption:

Year of deathFederal return required above
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

Plain, modest estates stay far below it. You subtract mortgages and other debts, the cost of administering the estate, and anything left to a spouse or a qualified charity. A widow or widower can also pick up the unused exemption of the person who died, by making an election on a timely return.

Real estate counts at what it was worth on the day of death, not the owner's old purchase price.

Most families never get a bill because of the unified credit, which ties the federal gift tax and estate tax into one system and rises with inflation each year. Gifts made during life count too: taxable lifetime gifts, beginning with 1977, are added back to the net estate before the tax is figured.

Selling an inherited Colorado house

Heirs can owe income tax, but just on profit over their basis. Inherited basis is not the decedent's original cost, and IRS Publication 551 explains how it is set. Profit is what the house sells for, less selling costs, less that basis.

The federal break for home sellers covers up to $250,000 of gain, or $500,000 on a joint return. It requires that you owned the place and lived in it for at least 24 of the last 60 months. Heirs who never moved in fail that test, so whatever gain exists is taxable. Colorado starts its own income tax from your federal taxable income, so the federal answer flows through to the state return.

  • Have the house valued as of the date of death, for example by an appraiser, before it goes on the market.
  • Save the estate paperwork showing what each heir received.
  • If a Form 1099-S shows up, report the sale even when no tax results.

A sale shortly after death usually leaves little profit to report. Waiting while prices rise leaves more.

Withholding when a nonresident heir sells

A seller who lives out of state will usually see the closing agent hold back some money for income tax. The holdback is 2% of the price of the seller's interest or the seller's net proceeds, whichever is smaller, and it is sent to the state on form DR 1079. The Department of Revenue publishes nonresident guidance with the details.

Estates face a parallel rule. When a nonresident beneficiary is paid net income from Colorado real or tangible personal property, the estate's fiduciary withholds income tax from that payment on form DR 0104BEP. The rate is the applicable income tax rate for the year times the beneficiary's net Colorado property income.

Think of the holdback as a prepayment. The nonresident claims it on a Colorado return and gets a refund of any excess. Ask the closing agent ahead of time so the smaller proceeds check is expected.

Steps for selling an inherited house

Here is a workable order once the family is ready to let go of the property.

  1. Find out who may legally sign. Usually that is the personal representative, either named in the will or appointed by a judge. The court clerk in the decedent's county can say where the case stands.
  2. Get the value as of the date of death in writing and file it with the estate papers.
  3. Look in the county records for liens, unpaid property tax or a mortgage still open. Closing pays those out of the sale money.
  4. Choose a route: list it, sell it as is to a buyer who accepts its condition, or let one heir buy out the rest.
  5. At closing the title company records the deed, takes out any nonresident withholding and pays off what the estate owes on the house.
  6. Report the sale on the income tax return for the year, on the estate's or the heirs' side, using the 1099-S if you receive one.

No step here involves a Colorado estate tax payment.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Colorado houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What a cash sale can skip

An estate often carries a house nobody wants to fix up. Selling for cash as is can take several steps off the list: no listing prep, no showings while the family is out of state, no waiting on a buyer's mortgage approval and no repair requests after an inspection. The deed is still recorded and any liens are still paid at closing, but the timeline is shorter and the price is agreed once, with all heirs signing the same contract.

Talk to the estate attorney first so the right person signs and the proceeds are divided the way the will or the court directs.

Common problems with inherited houses

Most trouble comes from distance, the state of the house and timing. Heirs often live far away, and Colorado stretches across 64 counties from the Front Range to the Western Slope and the Eastern Plains. Which court handles the estate depends on where the decedent lived, within the state's 23 judicial districts.

  • Out of town heirs end up managing keys, utilities and insurance by phone.
  • A buyer's lender may refuse a house until it is cleaned out.
  • Every heir has to agree on a single buyer and price.
  • Hail and wildfire damage can hit many parts of Colorado.

A cash purchase as is can shorten all of this. We buy Colorado houses in whatever shape they are in, estate properties included, so cleanout and repairs are not conditions of the sale.

Frequently asked questions

Is there an estate tax in Colorado?

No. Nothing is collected for deaths after December 31, 2004, and no state filing is needed.

Does Colorado have an inheritance tax?

No. The 1927 inheritance tax became an estate tax in 1980, and that tax is no longer collected.

When does the federal estate tax apply to a Colorado resident?

When the gross estate plus certain gifts passes the yearly threshold, which is $15,000,000 for deaths in 2026.

Do heirs pay tax when they sell an inherited Colorado house?

Only on profit above their basis. The home sale exclusion can reduce it for an heir who lived there, and IRS Publication 551 covers inherited basis.

Is money withheld when a nonresident sells a Colorado house?

Usually. The closing agent holds back 2 percent of the price or the net proceeds, whichever is less, and remits it to the Department of Revenue.

How a Colorado eviction starts

An eviction begins with a written notice from the landlord. A court case can be filed only after the notice period runs out, so the clock matters well before anyone sees a judge. There are three pre-filing notices, and the landlord picks one based on why the tenant is being asked to leave.

NoticeCourt formTypical useTime given
Demand for ComplianceJDF 99 AFix a lease violation or pay past-due rent3 to 30 days, set by the rental agreement
Notice to Terminate TenancyJDF 99 BRepeated or substantial violations, criminal behavior, some non-renewals1 to 91 days, set by the agreement
Notice of No-Fault EvictionJDF 99 CDemolition, repairs, owner use, sale, declined new lease, late payment historyAt least 90 days

Every notice has to be in the tenant's primary language. A notice in the wrong language is an easy way to lose time.

Standard notice length under state law

For most residential tenants the statute sets a ten day period. C.R.S. 13-40-104 applies it when a tenant holds over after unpaid rent, after breaking a material lease condition, or after conduct that disturbs others or damages the property.

One case gets a shorter period. An exempt residential agreement, meaning a single-family lease from a landlord who owns five or fewer such homes and says so in the agreement, can use five days. Nonresidential and employer-provided housing agreements get three days.

The same section lists other situations that count as unlawful detention. A few matter to anyone selling a house:

  • A tenant who stays after a foreclosure sale under a power of sale, once title is perfected and the buyer demands possession.
  • A person who will not leave after the buyer under a court judgment makes a demand and the redemption period is over.
  • An heir or devisee who refuses to leave property that a personal representative has sold, after a demand.
  • A contract buyer who fails to perform and keeps possession after a demand.

The heir and devisee item is the one that comes up with inherited houses. A relative who will not move out after the personal representative sells the property can face an eviction case.

Filing the case

When the notice period is over, the landlord files in the county where the property sits. The filing package is the Complaint (JDF 101), the Summons (JDF 102) and a copy of the notice that was posted or delivered.

The person filing must be the person in interest, which means the owner or the landlord named as lessor in the lease. A property manager may need to show proof of authority.

Mediation is required in most residential cases. Under C.R.S. 13-40-110, a complaint is started on the standard form, and skipping the mediation step where it applies is an affirmative defense that can lead to dismissal without prejudice. The statute carves out certain tenants and landlords, so confirm the current rule before relying on it.

A dismissal without prejudice lets the landlord start over, and starting over adds weeks to any plan to sell.

Serving the tenant and how fast the case moves

Service has to be finished at least seven days before the hearing date printed on the summons. There are two routes.

  • Personal service. The sheriff in the county where the tenant lives or works, a private process server, or an adult who is not part of the case hands over the papers. An Affidavit of Service (JDF 98) is needed for each defendant.
  • Posting and mailing. If personal service fails, the papers can be posted on the main door of the dwelling, and the summons, complaint and answer form must be mailed by the day after filing. The Certificate of Mailing on JDF 102 goes back to the court.

The choice has money attached. A landlord who wants a money judgment for back rent must use personal service, while posting and mailing supports possession only.

A tenant who wants to fight the case files a written answer on JDF 103. If the tenant neither answers nor shows up, the court can enter a default judgment.

Defenses a tenant can raise

The best known defense is unlivable conditions under C.R.S. 38-12-503. It applies to a nonpayment case when the home was unfit to live in and the tenant gave written notice on JDF 104. The landlord then has five days to repair unless the tenant caused the problem.

The defense has a cost. The tenant must pay the rent due into the court registry, less allowed expenses, and a tenant who does not pay the full amount at filing is in default.

On attorney fees, the losing side pays only if the lease says so. If the lease is silent, each side covers its own.

For a seller, the takeaway is that an unrepaired house can turn a routine nonpayment case into a contested one. Dated repair requests and records of what was fixed become important evidence.

If the tenant stays after judgment

Once a court orders the tenant out, the tenant usually has 48 hours to leave. If the tenant is still there, the plaintiff fills out a Writ of Restitution (JDF 109) and returns it to the court for the judge's signature.

After it is signed, the plaintiff contacts the sheriff to schedule the removal, and the sheriff charges a fee for serving the writ.

If you are weighing a sale, add up the likely timeline before choosing a path:

  • Notice period: 3 to 30 days for a demand, up to 91 for a termination, 90 or more for no-fault.
  • Time to file and serve, with at least seven days before the hearing.
  • Hearing, judgment and the 48 hour window.
  • Writ, sheriff scheduling and removal.

Each stage can stretch, so tell your buyer or title company which stage you are in and update them as it changes.

Can I evict a tenant because I want to sell?

Yes, but only through the no-fault route with a long notice. JDF 99 C lists the reason as "The Landlord intends to stop renting and sell the home," under C.R.S. 38-12-1303(3)(d).

The move-out date has to fall after the lease term ends and be at least 90 days after the notice is served. If the landlord or the landlord's spouse is on active U.S. military duty, the minimum drops to 45 days. Service is by leaving a copy with the tenant or posting it in a conspicuous place at the home.

The form excludes certain tenants:

  • Tenants who have lived in the home less than a year, or whom the landlord does not know to be a tenant.
  • Tenants of a resident landlord who lives in or next to a single-family home, duplex or triplex.
  • Employer-provided housing, mobile home spaces and short-term rentals.

A buyer who plans to take the house with tenants in it should ask for the lease and any notices before closing.

Selling while an eviction is pending

An eviction does not have to finish before a house can be sold. An occupied house can be sold as is, and the sale contract decides who deals with the occupants. The eviction process controls how a tenant can be removed, not whether the owner can sell.

Owners who sell to a cash buyer often pick a closing date that fits the notice or court timeline. The buyer then takes the house after the occupant has gone, or takes it with the tenant in place. The right choice depends on the lease, the notice already served and the stage of any court case.

The deed that transfers the house is recorded with the county clerk and recorder, who collects the documentary fee. Under C.R.S. 39-13-102 that fee is one cent for each $100 of consideration, and nothing is due when the consideration is $500 or less.

None of this replaces advice from a Colorado attorney if a case is already filed. If you want to talk through a sale while a tenant is still in the house, we can look at the lease and the dates with you.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does a Colorado landlord have to give for a standard eviction notice?

The standard residential period under C.R.S. 13-40-104 is ten days. Five days applies to exempt single-family leases from landlords who own five or fewer such homes, and three days applies to nonresidential and employer-provided housing.

How long does a tenant have to move out after the judge rules?

Usually 48 hours. If the tenant stays, the landlord files a Writ of Restitution (JDF 109) and the sheriff schedules the removal.

Can I sell my house while the tenant is still living in it?

Yes. A sale does not require the home to be empty, and the contract decides whether the buyer takes the house with the tenant or after the tenant has left.

How much notice does a landlord need to give if the house is being sold?

At least 90 days after service, and the move-out date must fall after the lease term ends. It can be as short as 45 days if the landlord or spouse is on active military duty.

Do I need to serve the tenant personally to get back rent?

Yes. Personal service is required to seek a money judgment, while posting and mailing supports possession only.

What a Colorado quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer happens to hold in a property and promises nothing about whether the title is good. Under C.R.S. 38-30-113 the deed has no warranty words, uses "quitclaim(s)" where other forms say "convey(s)", and passes no after-acquired title.

That last point is easy to miss. If the grantor later gets a better interest in the same property, a quitclaim does not pass it to the grantee. A bargain and sale deed does, and that is one of the real differences between the forms.

A properly executed deed in any of the listed forms conveys the property, and the form does not shrink the fee simple estate unless the deed reserves something.

Quitclaim compared with other Colorado deeds

The four statutory forms in C.R.S. 38-30-113 differ mainly in how much the grantor promises.

  • Warranty deed: includes the words "and warrant(s) the title to the same" and covers the property's whole history.
  • Special warranty deed: warrants the title only against people claiming under the grantor, so the promise covers the grantor's own period of ownership.
  • Bargain and sale deed: no warranty, but it does pass after-acquired title.
  • Quitclaim deed: no warranty and no after-acquired title.

A warranty or special warranty deed may be made "subject to statutory exceptions." Those are real estate taxes for the year of conveyance and later years not yet due, matters disclosed by a survey or inspection, and matters recorded with the county clerk and recorder. A quitclaim makes none of these promises to begin with.

What the deed must include

The deed has to identify the property precisely, name the right people and be acknowledged before a notary. The recording office wants the full legal description, and it should mirror the county's records.

  • Owners: when adding someone to a title, list everyone who needs to be on it, not only the new person.
  • Legal description: copy it from the county's records, not from a street address.
  • Notary: the notary must complete the entire notarial section.
  • Grantee address: C.R.S. 38-35-109 says deeds dated after January 1, 1977 must include the grantee's legal address, and a deed without it is returned for recording.

The deed statute itself is looser. It says leaving out an address or county of residence does not invalidate the deed. The two rules cover different points, validity in one case and recordability in the other, so supply the address anyway.

Margins matter too. Under C.R.S. 30-10-406, Gunnison County asks for a top margin of at least one inch and at least half an inch on the other sides, and a clerk may refuse a document that does not conform.

Where to record it

Record the deed with the clerk and recorder of the county where the land lies. C.R.S. 38-35-109 says deeds and court orders affecting title are recorded there, and it treats filing and recording as the same thing.

Colorado has 64 counties. A house in Colorado Springs goes to El Paso County and a cabin in Gunnison County goes there, no matter which county the owners live in. El Paso's Recording Department can be reached at 719-520-6200 or recweb@elpasoco.com.

What recording costs

In El Paso County a completed quitclaim deed records for a flat $43, covering every document regardless of page count. The flat fee took effect July 1, 2025, under House Bill 24-1269.

Piece of the El Paso feeAmount

Electronic Recording Technology Board surcharge$1.00

Gunnison County also charges $43 for a standard document and $0 for a death certificate, and El Paso records death documents into the real estate records free. Gunnison adds that card payments carry a vendor surcharge of at least $2.00 or 3.5%. Each office publishes its own rules, so check your county's schedule before you send anything.

Documentary fee

Yes, when a deed conveys ownership for money. Any document conveying real property pays the state documentary fee under C.R.S. 39-13-102, set at $0.01 per $100, which equals $0.10 per $1,000.

Transfers of under $500 are exempt. The Transfer Declaration, form TD 1000, accompanies the deed, is not recorded and is kept confidential. Ask the recording office whether the fee applies to your transfer.

Why recording matters

An unrecorded deed can lose to a later recorded one. C.R.S. 38-35-109 says an unrecorded instrument is not valid against anyone with rights in the property who records first, with exceptions for the parties themselves and anyone who had notice.

The same section adds a penalty. A person who records a document they know or have reason to know is forged, groundless or invalid can owe at least $1,000 or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees. If a relative asks you to sign a quitclaim to clear up a loan or a dispute, read it and understand what it does before you sign.

When a quitclaim works and when it falls short

A quitclaim suits transfers between people who already trust each other, such as adding a spouse or moving a house into a family arrangement. It falls short when a buyer needs a promise about the title, because the grantor gives none.

  • Works for: moving a known interest from one family member to another, and cleaning up the name on an existing title.
  • Falls short for: a sale to an outside buyer who expects title warranties, or any case where the title history is unclear.
  • Does not fix: unpaid property tax, liens or a loan tied to the property. Ask the lender, the title company or an attorney.

When heirs inherit a house and one sibling wants out, a quitclaim from that sibling to the others can move the interest. If the estate still has to be opened first, the title may not belong to the signer yet. Colorado's probate rules decide who can sign for an estate, and our Colorado probate guide covers that side.

Selling after a quitclaim

You can sell, but the buyer's title company will look at how title reached you. A seller who received the property by quitclaim has to show that the chain of recorded deeds supports a sale.

People in that position often choose a cash buyer who buys as is, since there are fewer repairs and showings to manage while the paperwork is checked. If the contract calls for a warranty or special warranty deed, the seller makes the title promises that a quitclaim leaves out, so read the deed form before closing.

Plan on three things before the closing date: a copy of the recorded quitclaim, a look at the recorded deeds that came before it, and a payoff for any loan or tax still attached to the house. The title company can tell you what else it needs.

Frequently asked questions

Does a Colorado quitclaim deed guarantee clear title?

No. Under C.R.S. 38-30-113 a quitclaim has no warranty words and passes no after-acquired title, so the grantor promises nothing about the title.

How much does it cost to record a deed in El Paso County, Colorado?

A completed quitclaim deed records for a flat $43. That is a $40 fee, a $1 ERTB surcharge and a $2 electronic filing surcharge, effective July 1, 2025.

Does the notary have to complete the whole section?

Yes. The recording office requires the notary to complete the entire notarial section of the deed.

Do I pay a documentary fee on a quitclaim deed in Colorado?

Possibly. A document conveying real property pays the state documentary fee of $0.01 per $100 under C.R.S. 39-13-102, with transfers under $500 exempt, and the TD 1000 declaration accompanies the deed.

Where do I record a Colorado quitclaim deed?

With the clerk and recorder of the county where the land is located. For Colorado Springs, that is the El Paso County Recording Department at 719-520-6200.

Beneficiary deeds in Colorado

Colorado calls it a beneficiary deed. It names who gets a house when the owner dies, and under C.R.S. 15-15-401 the owner can revoke it and the conveyance takes effect at the owner's death.

The person who signs is the owner, and the person named is the grantee-beneficiary. A successor grantee-beneficiary can also be named to take if the first choice does not outlive the owner. The rules are in Part 4 of Article 15 of the Colorado Probate Code, sections 15-15-401 through 15-15-415.

Most people look into one of these because they want the house to skip probate. A beneficiary deed is not a will, and it cannot be thrown out for failing the formalities that apply to wills (15-15-412).

Statute sections at a glance

Each section in Part 4 answers one question.

Statute sectionWhat it covers
15-15-401Definitions of beneficiary deed, owner and grantee-beneficiary
15-15-402Recording before death, no consideration, owner keeps control
15-15-403Medicaid eligibility
15-15-404Form of the deed and recording before death
15-15-405Revoking a beneficiary deed
15-15-406Acknowledgment
15-15-407Vesting of title and later claims
15-15-408Joint tenants
15-15-410Protection for a buyer from the grantee-beneficiary
15-15-411Time limits on claims
15-15-412Not a testamentary disposition

Statute text gets amended, so have an attorney or the county clerk confirm that nothing has changed before you rely on a section.

What must happen before the owner dies

The deed has to be recorded during the owner's lifetime with the county clerk and recorder where the house sits. The sample form in section 15-15-404 says in capital letters that the deed must be recorded before the grantor's death to be effective.

Other points from the statute:

  • No payment from the beneficiary is required, because no consideration is needed.
  • The beneficiary does not have to sign, agree or be told before the owner dies, though the beneficiary may still disclaim the property.
  • The deed has to meet the notarization and acknowledgment rules in 15-15-406, which point to C.R.S. 38-35-109 and 38-35-101.
  • Unless the owner says otherwise, the deed carries no title warranties and works like a bargain and sale deed.

The sample form also tells the assessor and treasurer that the beneficiary's address is only for identification. Tax notices keep going to the owner while the owner is alive.

Recording cost

Recording is a county charge. Denver and Delta County both list a $43 fee per document. Denver also asks for one-inch top margins and half-inch side margins, and says mailed documents can take 7 to 10 days while e-recording takes minutes.

Other counties set their own fees and habits, so call the clerk in the county where the house sits before you mail anything. Delta County records death certificates and verification-of-death documents in the real estate records at no fee, which helps later when a beneficiary needs the death on record.

Can the owner still sell after signing?

Yes. While the owner is alive the beneficiary has no right, title or interest, and the owner keeps full power over the property without the beneficiary's signature, consent or notice (15-15-402).

A homeowner who recorded a beneficiary deed years ago can still list the house, take a cash offer, refinance or pledge it. A normal sale deed signed by the owner passes title to the buyer, and the old beneficiary deed has nothing left to transfer once the house is gone.

Families sometimes get stuck because they believe the named beneficiary has to approve a sale. While the owner is alive, the statute says the opposite. If the owner has lost capacity, the question becomes who has authority to sign, and that is a job for an attorney.

Canceling or changing a beneficiary deed

The owner signs and records a written revocation before death. Under 15-15-405 it must describe the property, revoke the deed, and be recorded with the clerk and recorder in the county where the property is located.

  • The beneficiary does not need to sign or be notified.
  • A new beneficiary deed for the same property revokes all earlier ones, even if it covers only part of the owner's interest.
  • If several deeds or revocations are recorded before death, the one signed most recently controls, whatever the recording order.
  • A will cannot revoke or change a beneficiary deed that follows the statute.

The will point catches families by surprise. A will that leaves the house to one child does nothing against a recorded beneficiary deed naming another.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Colorado houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Joint tenants and Medicaid

A joint tenant can use a beneficiary deed, but title passes to the named person only if that joint tenant is the last surviving joint tenant (15-15-408). The deed does not break the joint tenancy.

Medicaid is the other trap. Section 15-15-403 says a person applying for or receiving medical assistance cannot qualify while holding an effective beneficiary deed where the state could assert a repayment claim, and signing one while applying makes the property a countable resource.

Section 15-15-407 adds that the beneficiary's interest is subject to the state's claims to recover medical assistance payments. Anyone near a nursing home or Medicaid decision should get advice before recording a deed or leaving one in place.

What happens when the owner dies

Title vests in the beneficiary only at the owner's death, and the beneficiary takes the owner's interest subject to existing liens, later interests and interests the beneficiary knows about (15-15-407). A mortgage stays with the house, and a deed of trust the owner signed does not vanish because a beneficiary deed exists.

Several time limits start running:

  • Holders of unrecorded interests must record a notice within four months after the owner's death (15-15-407).
  • Creditor claims against the owner are barred one year after death (15-15-411).
  • Other claims by heirs or devisees are barred at the earlier of three years after death or one year after the death is recorded in the county (15-15-411).
  • The beneficiary's interest stays subject to the state's Medicaid recovery claim (15-15-407).

Fraud is the exception to the time limits, since 15-15-411 does not bar an action to recover property obtained by fraud.

Selling the house after inheriting it

Once title has vested, the beneficiary can sell like any other owner, and a buyer or lender who pays value without notice is protected under 15-15-410. That buyer takes the property free of the rights of interested persons in the estate, and a recorded transfer showing the state documentary fee is prima facie evidence the transfer was for value. The beneficiary stays answerable to the estate's personal representative for duties under 15-15-103.

In practice, buyers and title companies want to see the recorded beneficiary deed, proof of death on record, and a clean payoff for any loan.

If you inherited a Colorado house through a beneficiary deed and want to sell it as is, call us for a written cash offer. Decisions about debts, other heirs and Medicaid recovery belong with an attorney.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Questions to settle before relying on a beneficiary deed

  • Is the deed recorded in the right county, and was it recorded before the owner died?
  • Was it signed and acknowledged to the standard in 15-15-406?
  • Does a later deed or revocation exist that was signed after this one?
  • Was the owner on Medicaid, or planning to apply?
  • Are there loans, tax bills or unrecorded claims on the house?

A title company can search the recorded documents for the answers to the first, third and fifth questions. If the answer to the fourth is yes, bring in an attorney before anyone signs a contract to sell.

Frequently asked questions

Is a beneficiary deed the same as a transfer on death deed in Colorado?

Yes. Colorado statutes use the term beneficiary deed, and it does the work other states call a transfer on death deed. It conveys the owner's interest at death and can be revoked while the owner lives.

Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?

No. Section 15-15-402 says the beneficiary does not need to join in, sign, consent to or be notified of the deed before the owner dies. The beneficiary may still disclaim the property.

Does a will override a beneficiary deed in Colorado?

No. Under 15-15-405, a beneficiary deed that follows the statute cannot be revoked or changed by the owner's will. Revocation takes a recorded written instrument signed before death.

Can I sell my house if I recorded a beneficiary deed?

Yes. While you are alive the beneficiary has no interest, and you keep full authority over the property under 15-15-402 without anyone else's consent.

What if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

Anti-lapse rules do not apply to beneficiary deeds. If one of several beneficiaries dies first with no alternate named, that share goes to the surviving beneficiaries in proportion, and a named successor grantee-beneficiary can be designated, so check how the deed was written.

How Colorado probate works

Probate is a district court process. The court appoints a personal representative, who collects the deceased owner's assets, pays valid debts and passes what is left to the heirs or devisees. Filers choose the type of case themselves, because the court cannot make that decision for them.

The arc is the same in nearly every estate. A representative is appointed, creditors are notified, assets are valued and sold or distributed, and the case closes once debts, distributions and tax returns are finished. For a family holding an inherited house, the practical point is that nobody can sign a sale contract for the estate until someone holds that authority.

A will should be lodged with the district court where the decedent lived within ten days of death, even if no administration is expected. That figure comes from an older publication, so ask the court clerk to confirm the current deadline.

Which court handles the estate

Open the estate in the district court of the county where the deceased lived. If the person lived out of state, file in any Colorado county where they owned property, which matters for a family inheriting a cabin or rental in the mountains. Denver is the exception, since estates there go to the Denver Probate Court.

Colorado has 64 counties, and Denver and Broomfield are consolidated city-counties. The county you start in depends on where the owner lived, not where the house sits.

Anyone who files without a lawyer is held to the same rules as an attorney. That is worth weighing before you start a formal case over a house with a mortgage and a buyer waiting.

Informal or formal probate

Informal probate is reviewed by the probate registrar with no hearing. Formal probate is reviewed by the court, and interested people can object before approval. There are four paths, each with its own forms.

  • With a will, informal: JDF 910, with instructions in JDF 906. No notice is required before the case is accepted.
  • With a will, formal: JDF 920, which is required if you only have a copy of the will.
  • Without a will, informal: JDF 916, with instructions in JDF 907.
  • Without a will, formal: a petition for intestacy on JDF 922.

Informal cases fit a valid will or a clear intestacy where no contest is expected. Formal cases suit disputes, unclear wills or trouble finding heirs. When a house is the main asset and the siblings disagree about selling it, formal probate is the usual route, and it takes longer.

Does a Colorado house always go through probate?

No. Only property held in the decedent's sole name without a beneficiary designation is controlled by the will. Jointly owned real property and assets with beneficiary designations, such as life insurance or IRAs, pass outside probate.

Even so, all wills and intestate estates must be probated, with the level of court involvement varying. A house titled only to the person who died is the typical case that needs a personal representative before it can be sold.

The small estate affidavit is the shortcut people ask about. It is available only when no real estate has to be transferred, and the affidavit form (JDF 999) is not filed with the court. State law at C.R.S. 15-12-1201 also requires at least ten days to have gone by since death and that no petition to appoint a personal representative is pending or granted anywhere. If the estate owns a house outright, plan on a regular case.

Probate deadlines

The first deadlines come fast. A case can be filed 120 hours after death, and once appointed, the representative has 30 days to notify interested persons and 90 days to prepare an inventory.

The inventory is not filed with the court, but beneficiaries who ask for it are entitled to a copy. Keeping it current helps when a buyer's title company asks what the estate owns.

How creditors are paid when the estate owns a house

The personal representative gives creditors notice and pays valid claims before distributing what remains. Under C.R.S. 15-12-801, the representative publishes notice in a newspaper in the county and may also mail written notice to a known creditor.

A creditor who gets written notice must present a claim by the later of the date in the published notice or 60 days after the notice is mailed or delivered, and in any case within one year of death. A creditor who misses the deadline is barred.

A secured lender is different. It can enforce a lien by foreclosure without filing a claim, so a mortgage on the inherited house does not wait on the claims period.

The deadlines in C.R.S. 15-12-803 cannot be waived or tolled. That is one reason heirs who want a quick sale still need the representative to follow the notice steps.

Selling the house before probate closes

Yes, once a personal representative has been appointed. Selling, transferring or encumbering real property is among the representative's powers, and the representative must inventory real and personal assets with titling and date-of-death values.

Informal and formal probates stay open at least six months. A sale can happen sooner, but the case itself will outlast the closing. Meanwhile carrying costs continue. El Paso County's treasurer, for one, charges interest of 1% per month on late tax payments with no grace period.

  • Real estate taxes: the bill goes to the owner of record, and not receiving it does not excuse late payment.
  • Mortgage: the lender can proceed on its lien regardless of the creditor claims period.
  • Insurance and upkeep: someone has to pay for them while the estate is open.
  • Time spent: a representative should track hours, since reasonable compensation is allowed.

A cash buyer that purchases as is can shorten the stretch between appointment and closing, because the house needs no repairs or showings first. The representative still signs, and the sale still follows the court's rules for the estate. A formal case may require court approval of transactions, so heirs who disagree should talk to a lawyer before any contract is signed.

What Colorado probate costs

The court charges a filing fee, so ask the clerk for the current amount. Filers who cannot pay can request a waiver with JDF 205 and the caption of JDF 206.

Other costs come out of the estate itself: attorney fees, final expenses of the decedent and legitimate debts. Attorneys usually bill hourly, with rates that depend on experience, difficulty and results. Selling a house adds its own closing costs, so heirs should ask for a written estimate before choosing an approach.

Problems with inherited Colorado houses

Inherited houses often arrive with an aging roof and deferred maintenance, and hail and wildfire are real risks in many parts of the state. Heirs who live elsewhere, own the house jointly or cannot afford a roof replacement often choose to sell as is.

The personal representative should confirm that insurance is active before listing the house or accepting any offer.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell a house in Colorado after someone dies?

Usually yes, if the house was in the deceased person's name alone with no beneficiary designation. Jointly owned real property passes outside probate, and the small estate affidavit does not cover real estate transfers.

How soon can I file for probate in Colorado?

Filing can happen 120 hours (five days) after death, and the court cannot act before then. A creditor who wants to open an estate must wait at least 45 days.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a Colorado estate?

A creditor who gets written notice has the later of the published period or 60 days from mailing, but no more than one year after death. Claims that arise after death must be presented within four months.

Which court do I file in for a Colorado estate?

File in the district court of the county where the person lived, or the Denver Probate Court for Denver. If the person lived out of state, file in any Colorado county where they owned property.

Can the personal representative sell the house without all heirs agreeing?

The representative has the power to sell, transfer or encumber real property. A formal case may require court approval of transactions, so a dispute among heirs usually calls for a lawyer's advice before any sale.

Colorado tax on house sale profit

No standalone capital gains tax exists in Colorado. Profit on a house lands in ordinary income, since the state begins with your federal taxable income and applies its own additions and subtractions. The state's Individual Income Tax Guide lays out that starting point.

One rate applies. C.R.S. 39-22-104 imposes 4.40 percent on federal taxable income for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2022, subject to the exceptions it names. Check the current Colorado return booklet for the rate in the year you sell, since the statute refers to other provisions that can change the rate actually charged.

Work out the federal result first, then layer Colorado's adjustments on top. If your federal return shows no taxable gain on the house, Colorado normally shows none either.

Federal exclusion that Colorado follows

A typical owner-occupant pays no tax on profit up to $250,000, or $500,000 when spouses file together. The IRS explains the rule in Topic 701, and Colorado inherits the result.

Two tests look back over the five years that end on closing day:

  • Ownership: the house was yours for at least 24 months.
  • Use: it was your residence for at least 24 months.
  • The two stretches can fall on different months.

With a joint return, one spouse can satisfy ownership, but each must satisfy use. Skip the exclusion if you already claimed one on another home in the prior two years. Service members, Foreign Service staff and intelligence personnel on extended duty can pause that five year window for up to 10 years.

You may still have to report. A Form 1099-S in your mailbox means the sale goes on the return even if every dollar of gain is excludable, and any gain you cannot exclude must be reported too.

Which Colorado sellers are most likely to owe tax?

The sellers with an actual bill are landlords, owners who moved away long ago, heirs who rent the house before selling and flippers. If the house was never your main home, the use test fails and the whole gain is taxable.

If the buyer pays part of the price in a later year, the installment method applies unless you elect out, and you can still use the exclusion.

Selling a Colorado house from out of state

Colorado taxes gain from real property located in the state even if you live elsewhere. The state's part-year resident and nonresident guidance treats income from Colorado real property, including capital gains and losses, as Colorado source income.

Expect withholding at the closing table. When a nonresident conveys Colorado real property, the title or settlement company usually keeps back two percent of the price of the seller's interest, or the seller's net proceeds if that is smaller, and remits it with form DR 1079.

  • Withholding is an advance payment, not the final bill.
  • Enter it on the Colorado return on the DR 1079 line rather than the W-2 line.
  • Any excess over the tax due can come back as a refund.
  • The credit for tax paid to another state is closed to nonresidents.

Form DR 1083 and its instructions cover the withholding in more detail. A seller who expects little or no gain should raise it with the title officer early.

Colorado subtractions that can reduce the gain

A few narrow subtractions exist, and only some involve real estate. One removes the slice of gain that arises because Colorado basis in a property is higher than federal basis. Another removes income Colorado taxed in an earlier year, so no dollar is taxed twice.

The only capital gain subtraction tied to a property type covers agricultural land, and only farmers who meet the acquisition and holding rules can use it. A town house or city lot is out.

Wildfire mitigation, such as clearing defensible space around structures, has its own subtraction. It reduces income for work you paid for and does not shrink the sale gain, yet it may matter if you spent money on mitigation before listing.

Figuring your profit

Start with the sale price, take away selling costs, then take away adjusted basis. Topic 703 describes basis as roughly your purchase price, plus improvements that add value, minus depreciation and casualty reimbursements.

  • Count a new roof, an addition or a finished basement.
  • Hold on to the closing statement from your purchase.
  • Subtract depreciation if the house was ever a rental.
  • An inherited house usually carries a different basis than the purchase price your parent paid. IRS Publication 551 covers gifts and inheritances.

Take a married couple filing jointly who lived there for 10 years. They can exclude up to $500,000. Profit below that line means no federal tax and none in Colorado. Profit above it is taxed, with the Colorado rate stacked on the federal one.

When you pay Colorado tax on the sale

Payment comes with your return, or earlier through estimated payments. Quarterly Colorado estimates are generally due once liability, after withholding and credits, passes $1,000.

The filing trigger mirrors the federal one: a federal filer, or anyone owing Colorado tax, files in Colorado. Nonresidents and part-year residents with Colorado source income file under the same test.

This page covers state income tax only. Run your own numbers past a tax preparer.

Steps before you sell

A short checklist keeps the tax side of a Colorado sale from surprising you at closing.

  • Count your months of ownership and of living in the house across the last five years.
  • Add up improvement costs and subtract any depreciation you took.
  • Decide whether the sale will be reported on a joint or single return.
  • If you live outside Colorado, ask the title company how it will handle withholding.
  • Set aside money for estimated payments if you expect a taxable gain.

What a cash sale changes

Taxes on the profit are identical whether the buyer pays cash or finances. The federal and Colorado rules attach to the price you accept.

Timing and cost are where a cash deal differs. An as-is sale skips repair spending and months of carrying costs, and a quick close may keep you inside the two year windows you were counting on. Sitting close to the 24 month mark? Check with a tax professional before signing.

Before accepting an offer, collect your purchase closing statement, receipts for major improvements and any Form 1099-S you expect. A preparer needs them whether the sale closes in a week or a quarter.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Colorado capital gains tax on selling a house?

No separate capital gains tax exists. The gain is part of Colorado taxable income, which starts from federal taxable income, and the statute sets a 4.40 percent rate for tax years from 2022.

How much of my house sale gain can I exclude?

Up to $250,000 if single, or $500,000 on a joint return, if you owned and lived in the home at least 24 months of the five years before the sale.

Do I pay Colorado tax if I live in another state?

Yes, on gain from Colorado real property. The closing agent generally withholds the lesser of 2 percent of the sales price or your net proceeds, and you reconcile on a Colorado return.

Do I report a house sale if the gain is excluded?

Yes if you receive Form 1099-S. You must report the sale even when the gain is fully excludable.

Does Colorado have a capital gain break for farmland?

A subtraction exists for agricultural land, limited to farmers who meet the acquisition and holding rules. It does not apply to ordinary houses.
